content.title: About
content.content: Almond butter is a spread made by grinding almonds into a smooth paste. The lower‑sodium version (2298 mg sodium) retains the rich, nutty flavor while keeping the salt level modest, making it suitable for sodium‑restricted diets.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Almond butter is high in heart‑healthy monounsaturated fats, similar to whole almonds.
The low‑sodium version is popular among athletes for post‑workout recovery.
It can be found smooth or with crunchy almond pieces for texture variation.
2298 mg of sodium aligns with the recommended daily limit of about 2300 mg.
Almond butter is often used as a peanut‑butter alternative for those with peanut allergies.

items.title: Rich in vitamin E
items.content: Almond butter is one of the best plant sources of vitamin E, an antioxidant that protects cells from oxidative damage.

items.title: Provides healthy fats
items.content: It contains mostly monounsaturated fats, which support heart health.

items.title: Contains magnesium
items.content: Magnesium aids normal muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Provides protein and fiber
items.content: The spread supplies plant protein and dietary fiber, promoting satiety.

items.title: Lower sodium content
items.content: Reduced salt makes it appropriate for people monitoring their sodium intake.

items.title: Tree nut allergy
items.content: Almond butter can trigger allergic reactions in individuals sensitive to nuts.

items.title: High in calories
items.content: Like whole almonds, it is calorie‑dense, so portion control is advised.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Almonds contain oxalates, which may contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Use almond butter as a spread on toast, stir it into smoothies, oatmeal, or yogurt, incorporate it into baked goods, or drizzle over fruit. Choose the unsalted or low‑sodium version to keep sodium intake low.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the jar in a tightly sealed container in the refrigerator. For longer shelf life (over 3 months), keep it in the freezer to prevent fat oxidation.

content.title: About
content.content: Blue or Roquefort cheese dressing is a thick, aromatic sauce made from cream, mayonnaise and crumbled blue cheese. It has a distinctive sharp, slightly tangy flavor and a creamy texture, perfect for salads, vegetables, seafood and meat dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditional Roquefort cheese is produced from sheep's milk in the Roquefort region of France.
The characteristic blue veins come from Penicillium roqueforti cultures added to the sauce.
Combining cream and mayo makes the dressing more stable for storage than pure blue cheese.
Often served in restaurants as a dressing for Caesar salads with added blue cheese.
In the United States, blue cheese dressing ranks among the top‑10 most popular wing sauces.

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: Blue cheese provides a good amount of calcium, essential for bone and teeth health.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: The dressing supplies both dairy and animal protein that supports tissue repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains vitamins B2 and B12, which help with energy metabolism.

items.title: Probiotic potential
items.content: The mold cultures may contribute to a healthy gut microbiome, though the effect is modest due to high fat content.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Vitamin A and fat‑soluble antioxidants help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: High fat and calorie content
items.content: The dressing is rich in saturated fats and calories, so it should be consumed in moderation.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Contains dairy, making it unsuitable for people with lactose intolerance.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: May trigger allergic reactions in individuals allergic to dairy proteins.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Blue cheese is salty; those monitoring sodium intake should limit portions.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Use the dressing as a salad topping, dip for vegetable sticks, chicken wings, burgers, or fish. It also works well mixed into pasta, mashed potatoes, or as a dip for chips.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the dressing refrigerated at 2‑4 °C in a sealed container. After opening, it is usually good for 5‑7 days. Discard if it develops a sour smell or changes color.

content.title: About
content.content: Fruit coleslaw is a fresh salad made from thinly shredded cabbage, carrots and a variety of fruits (such as apples, pears, pineapple), tossed in a light yogurt or creamy dressing. It combines the crunchy texture of vegetables with the sweetness of fruit, creating a refreshing side dish or light meal.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditional coleslaw originates from American cuisine, but modern versions often incorporate exotic fruits.
Fruit coleslaw is popular on summer restaurant menus because of its freshness and bright flavor.
Cabbage used in the salad is rich in vitamin C and fiber, while the fruits add extra vitamins and antioxidants.
The salad can be prepared ahead of time, but it is best to add the dressing just before serving to keep the crunch.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Cabbage and most fruits provide vitamin C, which supports the immune system and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: Cabbage and apples supply dietary fiber that promotes healthy digestion.

items.title: Low‑calorie option
items.content: When made with a low‑fat yogurt dressing, the salad remains light and suitable for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Fruits such as pineapple and berries contain polyphenols that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Hydration support
items.content: The high water content of vegetables and fruits helps maintain the body’s fluid balance.

items.title: Fruit allergies
items.content: Some individuals may have allergic reactions to certain fruits like kiwi or pineapple.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Improperly washed cabbage can harbor pathogens; it should be rinsed thoroughly.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Sweet fruits increase the overall sugar level of the dish, which may be a concern for people with diabetes.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Fruit coleslaw is served chilled as a side dish, a light lunch, or a snack. It can be added to sandwiches, used as a wrap filling, or simply eaten with a spoon.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the prepared salad in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Add the dressing right before serving to keep the vegetables crunchy.

green-peas-frozen-cooked-with-oil.title: Green peas, frozen, cooked with oil

content.title: About
content.content: Green peas are young pea pods harvested before the seeds fully mature. In frozen form they retain most of their nutrients, and cooking them with a small amount of oil adds flavor and improves nutrient absorption.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Frozen green peas are a convenient way to add vegetables to meals quickly.
Peas belong to the legume family and are a good source of plant protein.
Freezing preserves B‑vitamins and vitamin C, although some loss can occur during later heating.
Peas were domesticated more than 7,000 years ago in the Mediterranean region.
In several cultures green peas are a traditional dish for New Year celebrations.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: One cup of frozen peas provides about 8 g of protein, supporting muscle maintenance and vegetarian diets.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes digestive health and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Peas contain folate, thiamine, and vitamin B6, which are important for metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Flavonoids and carotenoids in peas help combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports heart health
items.content: Low in saturated fat and rich in potassium, peas contribute to normal blood pressure.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to peas, ranging from skin rash to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared products often contain added salt; people monitoring sodium intake should check the label.

items.title: Gas formation
items.content: Legumes can cause bloating in sensitive individuals; increase portion size gradually.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Peas contain modest amounts of oxalates, which may be a concern for those prone to kidney stones.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat frozen peas with oil in a skillet, add them to soups, stews, salads, or serve as a side dish. They pair well with garlic, lemon, and fresh herbs.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep frozen peas in the freezer at –18 °C (0 °F) or lower. After thawing, use within 2–3 days and do not leave at room temperature for more than 2 hours.

hot-chocolate-cocoa-dry-mix-reduced-suga.title: Hot Chocolate (Dry Mix, Reduced Sugar, Non-Dairy Milk)

content.title: About
content.content: A dry mix for hot chocolate with reduced sugar, made with non‑dairy milk (soy, oat or almond). The mix dissolves easily in hot water or plant‑based milk, creating a rich, aromatic beverage with a smooth chocolate flavor without any dairy ingredients.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The mix contains cocoa mass enriched with plant protein, making it more nutritious than traditional powders.
Sugar reduction is achieved with stevia and erythritol, which do not raise blood glucose levels.
Non‑dairy milk provides natural vitamin D and calcium, often added through fortification.
The dry form allows storage for up to 12 months without loss of flavor or aroma.
Lactose‑free hot chocolate is suitable for vegans and people with lactose intolerance.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Cocoa is high in flavonoids, which help combat free radicals and support cardiovascular health.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Reduced sugar and natural sweeteners prevent sharp spikes in blood glucose.

items.title: Source of plant protein
items.content: Fortified plant milk adds protein that aids muscle recovery and promotes satiety.

items.title: Supports bone health
items.content: Calcium and vitamin D fortification help maintain strong bones, especially important for vegans.

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: Absence of lactose makes the drink suitable for those with lactose intolerance.

items.title: Allergy to plant ingredients
items.content: The product may contain soy, oat or almond; individuals with allergies should check the label.

items.title: Sensitivity to sweeteners
items.content: Some people may experience mild gastrointestinal discomfort from stevia or erythritol.

items.title: Caffeine content
items.content: Cocoa contains a small amount of theobromine, which can affect sleep if consumed in large quantities.

items.title: Calorie increase with rich milk
items.content: Preparing the drink with full‑fat plant milk can raise the overall calorie count.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Mix 2‑3 tablespoons of the dry mix into 250 ml of hot water or plant‑based milk, whisk until smooth. Optionally add a pinch of cinnamon, vanilla, or a small amount of plant‑based butter for extra creaminess.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the dry mix in an airtight container in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. Once opened, use within 3‑4 months.

macaroni-or-pasta-salad-with-crab-meat.title: Macaroni or Pasta Salad with Crab Meat

content.title: About
content.content: Macaroni or pasta salad with crab meat is a cold dish where cooked pasta (usually short shapes such as penne or farfalle) is mixed with tender crab meat, fresh vegetables, and a light dressing made from mayonnaise, yogurt, or olive oil. The dish is popular in summer menus and often served as an appetizer or light meal.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The crab meat used is often real sea crab, but many recipes use crab sticks made from surimi for affordability.
Traditional versions add cucumber, sweet bell pepper, and green onion for texture contrast.
The salad is frequently garnished with dill or parsley and sometimes a splash of lemon juice for brightness.
In Japan a similar dish exists—crab pasta salad—where the dressing includes soy sauce and rice vinegar.
The salad can be prepared ahead of time; pasta and crab retain their flavor in the fridge for 2‑3 days.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Crab meat provides high‑quality marine protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Sea crab contains beneficial omega‑3s that support cardiovascular health.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Crab is a good source of vitamin B12 and niacin, important for nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Moderate carbohydrate content
items.content: Pasta supplies complex carbs, offering sustained energy for active individuals.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: When dressed with light yogurt‑based or olive‑oil dressing, the salad is low in saturated fats.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Crab meat can trigger severe allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared crab sticks often contain added salt and preservatives, so monitor overall sodium levels.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: If crab meat is left at temperatures above 4 °C for more than 2 hours, bacterial growth risk increases.

items.title: Gluten in pasta
items.content: Traditional pasta contains gluten, making the dish unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the salad chilled as a standalone appetizer or as a side to fish, seafood, or light meat dishes. It is easy to eat with a spoon or fork and can also be used as a sandwich filling.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the salad in an airtight container in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C. Properly stored, it remains tasty and safe for up to 3 days. Before serving, you may add fresh lemon juice or herbs if desired.

content.title: About
content.content: Soft pretzels NFS are baked from wheat flour and yeast dough into knot‑shaped sticks. They feature a lightly salty crust and a fluffy, tender interior. Pretzels work as a stand‑alone snack or as an accompaniment to soups, salads, and dips.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The pretzel tradition began in Europe, while the soft version became popular in the United States in the early 20th century.
Because of the yeast leavening, soft pretzels retain more moisture than their crunchy counterparts.
The original recipe uses sea salt, but today you can find cheese‑flavored, spiced, and sweet‑filled varieties.
The word “pretzel” comes from the German “Brezel,” which is linked to the Latin “bracellus” meaning “little arm.”
Soft pretzels are often sold in “servings” weighing about 30‑40 g each.

items.title: Carbohydrate source
items.content: Soft pretzels provide quickly digestible carbs that can rapidly replenish energy after physical activity.

items.title: B‑vitamin content
items.content: Yeast‑based dough is rich in vitamins B1, B2 and B3, which support metabolism.

items.title: Iron
items.content: Wheat flour contributes a modest amount of iron, important for blood formation.

items.title: Low fat
items.content: Unlike many baked goods, soft pretzels are typically prepared with little added fat.

items.title: Fiber (in whole‑grain versions)
items.content: Whole‑grain soft pretzels can provide dietary fiber that aids digestion.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Pretzels made from wheat flour can trigger reactions in people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Rapidly absorbable carbs may cause a quick spike in blood sugar, so those with diabetes should limit portions.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: The salty crust can be an issue for individuals monitoring sodium intake.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Although low in fat, pretzels are calorie‑dense due to carbs; moderation is key.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Soft pretzels can be enjoyed plain, split and spread with cream cheese, hummus, or jam. They are often served with mustard, cheese dip, or used as a “sandwich” base for ham and cheese fillings.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep soft pretzels in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2‑3 days. For longer storage, refrigerate—they stay soft for about a week. Discard any pretzels that develop mold or an off‑odor.

content.title: About
content.content: Pudding is a dessert made from milk, eggs, and thickeners, often sweetened and flavored. Bread is a baked product from dough of flour, water, yeast, and salt. Together, pudding can be used as a filling or topping for bread, offering a soft, sweet texture that contrasts with the crusty loaf.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The earliest pudding recipes date back to ancient Rome, using milk, honey, and grains.
In the United Kingdom, pudding is synonymous with classic desserts like "Sticky Toffee Pudding".
Bread is one of the oldest foods, with evidence of production over 10,000 years ago.
There are more than 200 types of bread, varying by leavening method, shape, and ingredients.
Pudding can be steamed, baked, or cooked on the stovetop, depending on the desired consistency.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: Eggs and milk in pudding provide complete protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D
items.content: Dairy components supply calcium and vitamin D, supporting bone health.

items.title: Energy supply
items.content: Bread delivers quick‑acting carbohydrates that fuel physical activity.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain bread contains fiber that aids digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Bread, especially whole‑grain varieties, is rich in B1, B2, and B3 vitamins important for metabolism.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Some individuals may react to the milk or eggs used in pudding.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Sweetened puddings can raise blood glucose levels.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Wheat bread contains gluten, which is unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The combination of pudding and bread can be calorie‑rich, so portion control is advisable.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve pudding warm or chilled, spread it on a slice of whole‑grain bread, use it as a sandwich filling, or enjoy it as a dessert after a meal.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep prepared pudding in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Store bread in a bread box or paper bag at room temperature; for longer storage, freeze and reheat in the oven before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Lamb stew is a dish made from bite‑size pieces of lamb slowly cooked in a flavorful broth with vegetables and spices. The meat becomes tender and the sauce rich, blending the tastes of herbs, onion, carrot and tomato.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Lamb is a rich source of iron that is more readily absorbed than iron from beef.
Stewing preserves most of the flavor and nutrients because the juices are retained.
In Mediterranean cuisine lamb is traditionally stewed with rosemary, thyme and mint.
Some cultures believe that slow‑cooked meat is easier to digest.
Lamb stew is often served with couscous, rice or mashed potatoes.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Lamb provides complete protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Rich in iron
items.content: The iron in lamb is highly bioavailable and helps maintain healthy hemoglobin levels.

items.title: Source of zinc
items.content: Zinc supports immune function and wound healing.

items.title: Contains vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 is important for nervous system health and red blood cell formation.

items.title: Contains polyunsaturated fats
items.content: Lamb stew includes beneficial fatty acids that may support heart health.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to lamb.

items.title: High saturated fat content
items.content: Excessive intake can contribute to elevated cholesterol levels.

items.title: Risk of overeating
items.content: Stews are often served in generous portions, which can lead to excess calorie consumption.

items.title: Bacterial contamination if improperly stored
items.content: Leaving the stew at room temperature for too long may allow harmful bacteria to grow.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot as a main course with sides such as potatoes, rice, couscous or vegetable ragout. Lamb stew also works well in sandwiches, tacos, or as a filling for pies.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the stew to room temperature, then store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze portions for up to 2 months. Reheat thoroughly before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: A vegetable sushi roll is a nori-wrapped roll that replaces fish with a fresh mix of vegetables such as cucumber, avocado, carrot, bell pepper and lettuce. It is usually served with soy sauce, wasabi and pickled ginger, and is popular among vegetarians and those seeking a light, low‑calorie alternative to traditional sushi.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Vegetable rolls appeared in Japan in the 1970s as a response to growing demand for vegetarian cuisine.
Nori sheets are rich in iodine and B‑group vitamins.
The combination of fresh vegetables makes the roll a source of vitamins A, C and K.
In Japan vegetable rolls are often called “katsu‑mori,” which translates to “vegetable roll.”
Traditional soy sauce served with rolls is fermented for at least six months.

items.title: Rich in vitamins
items.content: The vegetables provide vitamin C for immune support and vitamin A important for vision.

items.title: Low‑calorie
items.content: One roll typically contains 150–200 kcal, making it a good choice for weight management.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: Fiber from the vegetables aids digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Nori contains omega‑3 fatty acids and antioxidants that benefit heart function.

items.title: Low sodium content
items.content: When soy sauce is used sparingly, the roll remains relatively low in salt.

items.title: Seaweed allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to nori.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Soy sauce can significantly increase sodium intake, which is undesirable for hypertension.

items.title: Food‑borne infection risk
items.content: If vegetables are not thoroughly washed, bacteria may be present in the roll.

items.title: Gluten in soy sauce
items.content: Traditional soy sauce contains wheat; gluten‑free versions should be used for celiac disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The roll is conveniently eaten with chopsticks, cutting off bite‑size pieces. Dip each piece in soy sauce, add a dab of wasabi for heat, and eat pickled ginger between bites to cleanse the palate.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store a prepared roll in an airtight container in the refrigerator for no more than 24 hours. For longer storage keep the ingredients separate and assemble the roll just before serving.
